summary:
Formosa stands under Argentina's national framework, which remains among the most permissive in the world on paper. Law 26.743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after passing the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and the Senate 55 to one abstention, allows a change of legal gender without surgery, without hormone treatment and without judicial approval; the United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region, and Argentina legalised marriage equality in 2010 as the first Latin American country to do so.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action rather than by repeal. A decree of 5 February 2025 issued by the government of President Javier Milei restricts minors' access to gender-affirming surgery and hormone treatment, and a second decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. Legal experts called the decree on minors illegal and unconstitutional and petitioned the courts to intervene.

Protection machinery has been withdrawn at the same time. Trans people hired under the 1% Trans Labor Quota were dismissed, and the federal anti-discrimination agency INADI was abolished, removing the national body that had handled discrimination complaints.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented high in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity during the year, a ten-year record and a 62% increase on 2024, averaging one every 38 hours. Perpetrators were mostly security-force personnel and unknown assailants in public space, with beatings the main modality. Institutional violence rose from 17 cases in 2024 to 64 in 2025, and 32% of 2025 incidents took place inside police stations or prisons. Forty-three per cent of perpetrators were strangers to their victims.

Trans and travesti sex workers report police violence that has worsened since President Milei took office, and activists say it is worst outside Buenos Aires, in the more conservative interior provinces. Formosa is one of those provinces, and it sits under the national picture with no local reporting infrastructure to generate separate records.

On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance removed by an appeal court in 2020; the gender-motivated-crime aggravator therefore does not apply in that case as it now stands.
tangentialFactors:
An Outright International country overview updated on 12 March 2026 records negative assessments on same-sex relations, on gender recognition and on organisation registration, indicating deterioration despite the statutory framework. Argentina's anti-discrimination protections run through national and provincial laws, but the national enforcement agency has been abolished.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán and for Lohana Berkins, said in interviews on 4 April 2025 that the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate. Agencia Presentes presented the 2025 hate-crime figures on 19 March 2026 as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.

Formosa shares the interior-province profile that activists identify as the worst environment for trans sex workers, so the capital-based activist accounts bear directly on conditions here rather than on a distant pattern.
localsOnly:
Residents who lost jobs under the 1% Trans Labor Quota have no INADI to whom to take a discrimination complaint, since the federal agency has been abolished. Provincial-level anti-discrimination remedies, if any exist in Formosa, are not addressed by the sources.

Trans people held in custody in Formosa are subject to the prison-housing decree issued in February 2025, which governs where transgender detainees are housed. The national data on institutional violence show 32% of 2025 hate-crime incidents occurring inside police stations or prisons, so detention carries a documented elevated exposure.

Nationals seeking to update identity documents do so under Law 26.743 without surgery, hormone treatment or a court order, a process unchanged by the 2025 decrees, which concern minors' medical care and prison housing rather than adult legal gender recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the litigation brought against the February 2025 decree on gender-affirming care for minors is not recorded in the available sources and remains unresolved here.

No Formosa-specific hate-crime statistics, police-incident records or provincial reporting body appear in the inventory; the province has no local reporting infrastructure, so the national 2025 figures are the only quantified evidence available for conditions in Formosa.

Whether Formosa province maintains its own anti-discrimination statute or provincial human-rights office, and how its civil registry applies Law 26.743 in practice, are not sourced and should be verified independently. The inventory also does not record any Formosa-specific incident of violence against a named trans person.
